Content: I'm the farthest thing from an expert or a hater but from what I've found by googling's that using ammonia as a hydrogen energy alternative don't seem like a great idea, especially if we look at the omitted downsides, it'd be kind of like making fossil fuels, difference being that the greenhouse gas produced from burning ammonia is not CO2, but it'd still be a greenhouse gas, which's the whole reason why CO2 is "bad", I feel like Big Oil could adopt Ammonia because it’s basically a fossile fuel but it's renewable, which may sound good but that would just be replacing one greenhouse gas producer with another, cheaper one. and incase I misunderstood and the ammonia is just for storing hydrogen, I've also found that cracking the hydrogen back out of the ammonia is rather inefficient and expensive as the ammonia has to go through something much more complex than simple combustion before it can be used to make energy, it'd basically need it's own substation where it's turned back into hydrogen and then moved a smaller distance to stuff for on demand burning, which sounds like a whole buncha infrastructure to support ammonia based energy storage, transportation and utilization.

A few of the down sides not mentioned: Batteries are large and expensive, and enough storage to power single city overnight would be a gargantuan undertaking. Hydrogen isn't just a little difficult to store - it leaks through solid metal, is extraordinarily flammable, and makes metals brittle over time so everything containing it will eventually leak. Ammonia is extremely volatile (ie, turns into a gas), flammable, and poisonous. 

Storing renewables is critical, but it's also really freaking difficult.

Author: @Markfr0mCanada
Content:
Certainly an important topic to talk about.  A major missed point is that every energy conversion has significant efficiency losses.

Your best system is one which minimizes the number of times energy is converted.  To this end, including hydro electricity in the production mix is likely to work best, as gravitational potential energy can be stored by slowing the rate which water passes through the turbines.  Changing the level in the artificial lake acts as a gravity batter.

And since somebody is going to bring up pump stored hydro electricity:  It's a nice idea, but under ideal conditions only returns 30%, so put 10 units of spare energy into storage and get 3 out when you need them.
